script: My 8‑year‑old revenge: I stole my mom's money and turned it on her.. I was eight when my mom started treating me like a disposable trash can. She'd buy me new clothes for her friends and me only got the rags that didn't fit. My siblings wore fresh tees while I wore the same crummy ones forever. She kept her hair and nails on point, but my hair never got brushed. The disability money she got? She spent it on her own things, not on me. She saw me as a money bag, not a kid. One day, my teacher noticed my hair was never brushed, my clothes never washed, and I was practically invisible in my old clothes. She asked what was up, and I spilled the whole truth. The next day she handed me new shoes, a brand‑new jacket, and even a hairbrush. Her daughter ran a charity for kids' clothes, so I got name‑brand gear. She even did my hair. (Micro‑hook: "I walked home in a brand‑new outfit, and my mom's face turned to a mask of disdain.") I came home wearing my new clothes. Mom gave me a dirty look and demanded where I got them. I said my teacher gave them. She exploded, "So now your teacher thinks she's better than me because she can afford nice things?" The audacity. She grounded me for a week and banned me from the family trip. I felt like a ghost. I wanted to run. I had this plan in my head that was, honestly, pretty clever for a kid. I was sweating like a marathon runner. I took my mom's pillowcases, rubbed them between my sweaty cheeks—those sheets were already a stench—and grabbed one of her favorite T‑shirts to wipe after using the bathroom. I had diarrhea too, so the smell was off the charts. Hours later I heard her gagging, talking about how nasty her shirt and pillow sheets smelled. I could feel the sting of my revenge. I didn't need to show off; I just needed to make her feel the same discomfort she'd always put on me. The moment she coughed, I knew I'd finally got a taste of power.
